description: We are a multidisciplinary team passionate about space exploration, science, and technology. We combine data analysis, programming, engineering, scientific research, design, and 3D modeling to develop innovative solutions using NASA's open data. Our goal is to transform complex ideas into functional prototypes that contribute to addressing the future challenges of space exploration.
summary:
We developed H.E.L.I.O.S., a lightweight software platform for the comprehensive preventive health monitoring of astronauts in deep space. It is a technological ecosystem that integrates already-validated wearable biomedical sensors (Intravehicular Activity [IVA] garment, continuous glucose monitors, and acoustic dosimeters), environmental telemetry regulated under NASA standards, the psychological assistant, and explainable algorithms to safeguard the crew's physical, cognitive, and emotional well-being.
The project addresses the five critical hazards of long-duration spaceflight—radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and closed habitats—adapting to transit spacecraft (0 g), orbital stations (LEO), and Martian bases (3/8 g). Unlike conventional systems that display isolated vital signs reactively, our architecture cross-references physiological, behavioral, and cabin variables through an explainable multivariable matrix to trigger personalized countermeasures before a medical emergency arises.   
This solution is indispensable because missions to Mars face communication delays of up to 22 minutes that prevent immediate medical support from Earth. Early mitigation of bone loss (up to 1.5% per month), neuro-ocular syndrome, acoustic fatigue, and decision overload ensures crew autonomy and the success of space exploration.
details:
What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

H.E.L.I.O.S. (Health Indicators and Environmental Life Observation System) is a lightweight, integrated clinical and preventive decision-support software platform designed for astronauts on long-duration space missions (0 g transit, Low Earth Orbit (LEO) stations, and Martian bases operating at 3/8 g).

Rather than developing new physical devices, H.E.L.I.O.S. operates as a hardware-independent intelligent layer that ingests, normalizes, and contextualizes telemetry from pre-existing, validated biomedical and environmental equipment, including Intravehicular Activity (IVA) garments, pulse oximeters, and cabin sensors regulated under NASA-STD-3001.

Its workflow consists of four stages:

  • Data Ingestion and Individual Baseline: Captures physiological, behavioral, and environmental data streams, continuously comparing them against each crew member’s historical profile to prevent false alarms.
  • Explainable Multivariable Matrix Correlation: Correlates cabin environmental variables (CO₂, O₂, radiation, and noise) with vital signs (heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), SpO₂, and skin temperature) and cognitive workload to identify root causes with transparent traceability, avoiding the opacity of “black-box” systems.
  • Preventive Countermeasures and Psychological Support: Upon detecting early deviations, the system activates personalized protocols (“Bone Shield,” visual health and fluid shift monitoring, hydration, or acoustic rest) and integrates a conversational assistant designed to apply cognitive reframing techniques and reduce decision-making overload in isolated environments.
  • Dual Interface and Autonomous Edge Operation: Operates locally without relying on continuous connectivity with Earth (critical during communication delays of up to 22 minutes with Mars) and provides an intuitive, actionable interface for astronauts alongside a comprehensive analytical dashboard for Flight Surgeons.

What Are the Benefits?

  • Continuous Physiological Monitoring Without Additional Hardware: Monitors key health indicators (heart rate, blood pressure, and blood oxygen saturation) using pre-existing medical devices, eliminating the additional spacecraft mass and launch costs associated with new hardware.
  • Psychological Well-Being Protection: Features an AI-powered conversational voice assistant that interacts with astronauts through daily check-ins, assesses their self-reported well-being, and identifies potential changes in emotional states and behavioral patterns.
  • Cabin environmental contextualization: Integrates spacecraft environmental conditions with vital signs to quickly distinguish whether a change is physiological or environmental.
  • Early detection via AI-powered data integration: Combines physiological, psychological, and environmental indicators, including information gathered through voice interactions, to identify deviations, emerging patterns, and potential relationships between different health factors.
  • Timely automated alerts: Flags potentially significant anomalies in real time so astronauts or medical personnel can promptly verify and assess them.
  • Optimized Flight Surgeon review time: Generates AI-assisted preliminary health reports summarizing relevant changes and patterns, streamlining remote clinical evaluation.
  • Personalized, accessible prevention: Delivers actionable recommendations (physical activity, mobility exercises, relaxation, and well-being routines) that ensure deep-space autonomy and can be easily downloaded for everyday telemedicine on Earth.

What is the expected impact of the project?

H.E.L.I.O.S. directly transforms health management in long-duration space missions—from current orbital stations to the Artemis program and future Mars expeditions—enabling autonomous clinical prevention against critical pathologies during communication delays without adding spacecraft mass. Furthermore, as a lightweight software that anyone can easily download and deploy on commercial wearables, its impact extends beyond spaceflight to democratize preventive health monitoring for remote telemedicine in isolated communities, high-altitude mining, and polar expeditions.

How is your project creative?

It bridges four domains that typically operate in silos—human physiology, behavioral psychology, cabin environment, and operational workload—into a single explainable decision engine. Instead of displaying passive charts or opaque algorithms, it translates complex cross-domain correlations into clear preventive actions dynamically recalibrated to the gravitational environment (0 g, LEO, or 3/8 g).

H.E.L.I.O.S. adds an AI-assisted psychological voice support system that provides daily conversational check-ins and personalized wellness recommendations. By analyzing astronauts' responses and relevant vocal characteristics alongside sleep patterns and other health indicators, it aims to identify potential changes in well-being. Suggesting adaptive routines, relaxation activities, and coping strategies, while flagging recurring concerns in preliminary reports for medical professionals. Helios offers an additional layer of daily support without replacing human interaction or professional psychological care.

What tools, coding languages, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Architecture: 100% Software-First
  • Development Tools: AI-assisted development tools (ClaudeGO) for code prototyping, architectural refinement, and technical documentation.
  • Frontend & User Interface: HTML5, JavaScript, CCS
  • Backend, Simulation & Analytical Engine: Phyton
  • AI & Conversational Assistant: Large Language Model integration (Gemini / GPT APIs) paired with clinical/psychological prompt engineering, structured safety guardrails, and an explainable rule-based analytical layer for offline (edge) resilience and preliminary health report generation.
  • Data Sources & Standards: NASA-STD-3001 (Spaceflight Human-System Standard, Volumes 1 & 2)

What factors did your team consider?

  • Spacecraft constraints (SWaP): Strict mass, volume, and power limits, addressed by leveraging already-qualified sensors.
  • Communication latency: Local (edge) processing to ensure clinical autonomy during up to 22-minute Mars delays.
  • Clinical explainability: Full traceability behind every alert so Flight Surgeons can audit and trust the system.
  • Human factors (NASA-STD-3001): Role-specific interfaces designed to prevent astronaut information overload.
